acts.title: The turning world, where every debt must find its shore

lines.dialogue: I must deliver this, or the lock-keeper will hold my boat for three more days.
lines.stage_directions: hands Wan an opened letter

lines.dialogue: The lock-keeper is my cousin. I told him to hold your boat.
lines.stage_directions: steps onto the veranda, carrying a sheet of blank paper

lines.dialogue: An unclaimed jar of a dancer’s ashes has sat at the wat for four years. Only a relative can make merit, and a woman alive on paper cannot have merit made.
lines.stage_directions: arrives

lines.dialogue: Nim, daughter, the remittance did not come. Is your hand well? I take the morning boat. I must give the boatman an answer before the boat arrives, or our letters stop.
lines.stage_directions: reads the letter aloud without looking up

lines.dialogue: We each know what is at stake.
lines.stage_directions: picks up his pen, looks at the blank paper, and puts it down

lines.dialogue: I will dictate the truth myself, but these hands cannot hold a pen now.
lines.stage_directions: her hands tremble as she holds the blank paper

lines.dialogue: Write it for me before the boat arrives.
lines.stage_directions: turns to Lek
opens his tin box and takes out a stack of practice sheets; every line is the same signature in a woman's neat hand. — a man who trusts handwriting more than speech.

lines.dialogue: A debt arrives on the third of the month. The Bangkok boat rounds the bend in an hour.

lines.stage_directions: leads Lek and The Dance Teacher away from the school veranda, down the canal-side path toward the funeral parlor.

line.dialogue: My boat is held on a cousin’s word. Do I wait for your letter or cast off now?

choices.description: I will give the Boatman the letter to hold for one more hour.

line.dialogue: I see him tie his boat to the veranda post.
I watch his boat pull away from the landing.

choices.description: I will ask the Boatman to tell the lock-keeper the letter is being written right now.

line.dialogue: I hear him call across the water that the letter is coming.
I see him shake his head and begin untying the rope.

choices.description: I will take the practice sheets and show the Boatman the signature to prove a letter comes.

line.dialogue: I see him nod at the signature and sit down on the gunwale to wait.
I watch him pocket the sheets and push off from the dock.

acts.title: The turning world, where every debt must find its shore

lines.stage_directions: stops at the pawnshop counter under the wooden awning.
slides a small, square cloth bundle across the counter without being asked.

lines.dialogue: The answer is here, in the metal and the string.
lines.stage_directions: unwraps the cloth: a woman’s thin gold bracelet, a faded red pawn string still knotted to one link.

lines.dialogue: I weighed it — the same weight, but not the same meaning.
lines.stage_directions: rewraps the bracelet and tucks it into his pocket.

lines.dialogue: The appraiser never asks why a thing comes or goes; his silence is a kind of promise.

lines.stage_directions: sits behind a counter, a clock ticking beside him.

lines.dialogue: We need the use of your back room. For one afternoon.
A ledger of love, kept in pigeonholes—the corrected price in black ink; the exact value of an afternoon's silence.
lines.stage_directions: quotes a price in red ink on a scrap, crosses it out, writes a lower one in black.
counts baht notes onto the table.

lines.dialogue: I taught only one dancer who could copy that hand. She is ash in a jar now.
Could one of your pupils sit veiled here this afternoon? To be the lady Nim for a mother’s visit.
A small gathering. Your veranda’s letter traffic makes for interesting reading." "I could strike a prison entry from the rolls… for copies of who sends money where.
lines.stage_directions: enters, followed by a clerk with a ledger.

line.dialogue: A bracelet comes and goes. Do you leave it as pledge or take it to show the mother?

choices.description: I will leave the bracelet with the Appraiser as security for the funeral parlor fee.

line.dialogue: I see him note the bracelet in his ledger and hand me a receipt.
I see him shake his head and slide the bundle back across the counter.

choices.description: I will show the bracelet to The Dance Teacher and ask if Nim ever wore it.

line.dialogue: I see her touch the gold and her eyes fill with water.
I see her turn away from the bracelet and say she does not remember it.

choices.description: I will take the bracelet from the Appraiser and show it to the mother before I pledge it.

line.dialogue: I see him wrap it carefully and put it in his own pocket.
I see him hand it back, saying he cannot carry a dead woman’s gold.

acts.title: The turning world, where every debt must find its shore

lines.dialogue: The veranda's letters are private stationery.
lines.stage_directions: lays a hand on the stack of practice sheets.

lines.dialogue: Here. The first entry is a Bangkok shophouse alley.
lines.stage_directions: opens the ledger on the table, pointing with a pen.

lines.dialogue: The boat will dock soon. Four satang a page to write a letter for someone else.
lines.stage_directions: glancing out the window.

lines.dialogue: Then I will go to the landing myself. I will tell the mother the truth.
lines.stage_directions: moving toward the door.

lines.dialogue: Four satang a page for a dictated letter. That is our work.
lines.stage_directions: stepping swiftly into her path, blocking the door.

lines.dialogue: The debt that flows uphill. The District Officer closes his ledger and looks toward the canal where the boat will arrive.
The Bangkok boat, tied at the landing below.
An old woman climbs the steps, holding a shophouse paper bag.

line.dialogue: My ledger is open. Do you show me the practice sheets or keep your silence?

choices.description: I will show the Officer one practice sheet with the signature to satisfy his curiosity.

line.dialogue: I see him nod and make a small mark in his ledger.
I see him take the whole stack and tuck it under his arm.

choices.description: I will offer to copy the shophouse alley entry from his ledger for my own records.

line.dialogue: I see him smile and point to the entry with his pen.
I see him snap the ledger shut and hand it to his clerk.

choices.description: I will tell the Officer the handwriting belongs to a woman who makes merit monthly.

line.dialogue: I see him pause, then turn the ledger page away from that entry.
I see him laugh and say merit cannot be entered in a district roll.

lines.stage_directions: places a small ceramic jar on the veranda rail.

lines.dialogue: An old woman calls out Nim’s name from the steps.
Mother. The elder of the two of us is not here today.
lines.stage_directions: steps forward and bows deeply

lines.dialogue: The old woman holds out the paper bag — mangoes and a new stone; the money stopped, so she wrote, but no answer came.

lines.stage_directions: takes the old woman's arm gently and guides her to sit on the veranda bench.
eyes move from the practice sheets, to the small jar on the rail, to the blank paper waiting on Wan's table.

lines.dialogue: Will you write the letter?
lines.stage_directions: lifts the pen from the inkwell.

lines.dialogue: The canal carries the mother’s boat, and will carry her back, in a world where handwriting outlives the hand.
Om.
lines.stage_directions: looks from the jar to the water.

line.dialogue: The jar holds ash. Do you place it before the mother or keep it on the rail?

choices.description: I will move the jar to the writing table where the mother can see it.

line.dialogue: I see her look at the jar and her hands go still on the paper bag.
I see her glance at it and then turn her face toward the canal.

choices.description: I will ask the Monk to carry the letter to the mother on the veranda.

line.dialogue: I hear him begin a chant and see the mother bow her head.
I see him remain silent and cover the jar with his robe sleeve.

choices.description: I will show the handwriting on the practice sheets to the Dance Teacher.

line.dialogue: I see her touch the ash with one finger and then nod to the mother.
I see her turn away and press her shaking hands over her ears.
